title: Cross-Layer Exploration and Chip Demonstration of In-Sensor Computing for Large-Area Applications with Differential-Frame ROM-Based Compute-In-Memory
problem: Thin-film technologies for large-area and flexible integration struggle to implement in-sensor computing due to low device performance, large-area integration variation, and costly sensor-CMOS processor interfaces.
motivation: In-sensor computing mitigates massive data transmission costs between sensors and processing units, crucial for large-area and flexible applications.
method: The system integrates processing circuits (a ROM-based compute-in-memory scheme using lookup tables for calculations) directly adjacent to the light sensors, enabling massively parallel image preprocessing. Differential-frame computing (comparing successive frames to detect changes) provides robustness and naturally creates data sparsity (abundance of zeros). A bio-inspired compression technique using residual recovery caches and zero-skip circuits further reduces data size without accumulated errors. The entire design uses LTPS TFT technology (low-temperature polysilicon thin-film transistors for large-area integration) with optimizations coordinated across all chip layers.
key_novelty: Differential-frame ROM-based compute-in-memory (a processing scheme that compares frames and uses lookup tables) integrated directly into image sensors built from thin-film transistors, combined with bio-inspired compression for data reduction without errors.
contributions: In-sensor computing architecture with compact ROM-based CiM enabling high parallelism for large-area applications
Differential-frame computing technique providing robustness and enhanced data sparsity
Bio-inspired compression method with residual recovery for zero-accumulated-error output
Fabricated LTPS TFT-based ROM CiM chip demonstrating 3.85× speedup and 5.10× energy efficiency over traditional architectures
